title: Housing & Moving
subtitle: Read the adverts, survive the viewing, share the flat and fix the place up

lessons.title: Chercher un logement
lessons.description: Decode French property adverts, ask the questions that matter at a viewing and put together a rental application file.

blocks.heading: Reading a French property advert
blocks.body: French adverts are written in a compressed telegraphic style: no articles, lots of abbreviations. T2 or F2 means two rooms not counting the kitchen and bathroom, so a T2 is a one-bedroom flat. Surfaces are always in square metres, and the rent is quoted either CC (charges comprises, service charges included) or HC (hors charges, excluding them). Learning to expand these codes into full sentences is half the battle.

examples.french: Loue T2 de 42 m², 3e étage avec ascenseur, 780 € CC.
examples.english: T2 for rent, 42 m², 3rd floor with lift, €780 including charges.

examples.french: Le loyer est de 650 euros hors charges.
examples.english: The rent is 650 euros excluding service charges.

examples.french: L'appartement fait quarante mètres carrés.
examples.english: The flat is forty square metres.

examples.french: Studio meublé, libre au 1er septembre.
examples.english: Furnished studio, available from 1 September.

examples.french: Appartement lumineux donnant sur une cour calme.
examples.english: Bright flat looking out onto a quiet courtyard.

examples.french: Proche métro et commerces, quartier bien desservi.
examples.english: Close to the metro and shops, well-served neighbourhood.

blocks.tip: Faire is the verb for measurements: la chambre fait 12 m². Avoid être here — l'appartement est 40 m² sounds wrong to French ears.

blocks.heading: The questions to ask at a viewing
blocks.body: A viewing lasts fifteen minutes, so your questions have to be sharp. The essentials are what the charges cover, what kind of heating there is, how long the lease runs and how much notice you must give. Use est-ce que or simple intonation questions — an agent will not mind, but vague questions get vague answers.

examples.french: Qu'est-ce que les charges comprennent exactement ?
examples.english: What exactly do the service charges cover?

examples.french: Le chauffage est individuel ou collectif ?
examples.english: Is the heating individual or communal?

examples.french: Quel est le montant de la caution ?
examples.english: How much is the deposit?

examples.french: Le bail est de combien de temps ?
examples.english: How long is the lease?

examples.french: Il faut donner combien de préavis pour partir ?
examples.english: How much notice do you have to give to leave?

examples.french: Est-ce qu'il y a du vis-à-vis depuis le salon ?
examples.english: Is anything overlooking the living room?

blocks.tip: Ask to see the diagnostic de performance énergétique (DPE): a flat rated F or G will cost a fortune to heat in winter.

blocks.heading: Putting your file together
blocks.body: In big French cities you rarely get a flat because you liked it — you get it because your dossier was the strongest. A dossier normally holds an ID, the last three pay slips, a tax notice and a garant, a guarantor who commits to paying if you cannot. Speak about it in the perfect and the near future: j'ai envoyé mon dossier, je vais signer demain.

examples.french: J'ai envoyé mon dossier dès la fin de la visite.
examples.english: I sent my file off as soon as the viewing was over.

examples.french: Il me manque encore un justificatif de domicile.
examples.english: I'm still missing a proof of address.

examples.french: Mon père se porte garant pour moi.
examples.english: My father is acting as my guarantor.

examples.french: L'agence demande de gagner trois fois le loyer.
examples.english: The agency requires you to earn three times the rent.

examples.french: On m'a dit que le dossier était accepté.
examples.english: I was told the file had been accepted.

examples.french: Je signe le bail vendredi et j'emménage samedi.
examples.english: I'm signing the lease on Friday and moving in on Saturday.

blocks.tip: Les frais d'agence are capped by law and are paid once, at signature. If someone asks for money before the viewing, walk away.

blocks.heading: Asking precise questions with quel and inversion
blocks.body: Quel is an adjective, so it agrees with the noun it questions: quel étage, quelle surface, quels travaux, quelles charges. With être it stands alone: quel est le montant ? For a slightly more formal register at a viewing, use inversion — comprend-il l'eau ? — while est-ce que and rising intonation stay perfectly acceptable. When a third-person verb ends in a vowel before il or elle, French inserts -t-: donne-t-elle sur la rue ?

examples.french: Quelle est la surface exacte du séjour ?
examples.english: What is the exact floor area of the living room?

examples.french: Quels travaux sont prévus dans l'immeuble ?
examples.english: What works are planned in the building?

examples.french: Le loyer comprend-il l'eau chaude ?
examples.english: Does the rent include hot water?

examples.french: La chambre donne-t-elle sur la cour ?
examples.english: Does the bedroom look out onto the courtyard?

examples.french: À partir de quand le logement est-il libre ?
examples.english: From when is the property available?

examples.french: Combien de temps faut-il pour avoir une réponse ?
examples.english: How long does it take to get an answer?

blocks.tip: Never mix quel with est-ce que and inversion at once. Quel est le loyer ? is right; quel est-ce que le loyer est ? is not French.

blocks.heading: Comparing two flats: plus… que, moins de… que, autant de
blocks.body: To weigh up two places, compare adjectives with plus / moins / aussi + adjective + que, and quantities with plus de / moins de / autant de + noun + que. Verbs take plus, moins or autant on their own: je paie moins que toi. Watch the irregulars: bon becomes meilleur, and bien becomes mieux. For superlatives, add the article: le quartier le plus calme, le loyer le moins cher.

examples.french: Ce studio est plus lumineux que l'autre.
examples.english: This studio is brighter than the other one.

examples.french: Il y a moins de bruit qu'au premier étage.
examples.english: There's less noise than on the first floor.

examples.french: L'appartement a autant de rangements que le précédent.
examples.english: The flat has as much storage as the previous one.

examples.french: C'est le meilleur rapport qualité-prix du quartier.
examples.english: It's the best value for money in the neighbourhood.

examples.french: Ici, on est mieux desservi qu'en banlieue.
examples.english: Here we're better served by transport than in the suburbs.

examples.french: C'est le loyer le moins cher que j'aie trouvé.
examples.english: It's the cheapest rent I've found.

blocks.tip: After a superlative, French often slips into the subjunctive: le seul appartement que j'aie visité. It sounds educated and is easy to imitate.

passages.title: Trois visites en une matinée
passages.french:
Samedi matin, j'avais rendez-vous pour trois visites d'affilée.
Le premier appartement, un T2 de quarante mètres carrés, était magnifique sur les photos.
En vrai, la chambre donnait sur un mur et le chauffage datait des années soixante-dix.
L'agent parlait vite : « Le loyer est de neuf cent vingt euros hors charges, il part aujourd'hui. »
J'ai posé mes questions habituelles : la surface exacte, le montant de la caution, la durée du bail.
Il a soupiré, comme si vouloir comprendre était une impolitesse.
Le deuxième était un studio exigu mais très lumineux, dans un immeuble rénové l'an dernier.
Aucun vis-à-vis, un vrai coup de cœur, sauf que le quartier est mal desservi le dimanche.
Le troisième, moins cher, se trouvait au sixième étage sans ascenseur.
J'ai renoncé avant même d'arriver en haut, mes cartons à venir en tête.
Le soir, j'ai envoyé mon dossier pour le studio : pièce d'identité, fiches de paie, garant.
Trois jours plus tard, l'agence m'a appelée pour me dire que c'était accepté.
Je signe le bail vendredi et j'emménage le week-end suivant, avec l'état des lieux en main.
passages.english:
On Saturday morning I had appointments for three viewings back to back.
The first flat, a 40-square-metre one-bedroom, looked magnificent in the photos.
In reality, the bedroom looked out onto a wall and the heating dated from the seventies.
The agent spoke fast: "The rent is nine hundred and twenty euros excluding charges, it'll go today."
I asked my usual questions: the exact floor area, the amount of the deposit, the length of the lease.
He sighed, as if wanting to understand were rude.
The second was a cramped but very bright studio, in a building renovated last year.
Nothing overlooking it, love at first sight — except that the neighbourhood is badly served on Sundays.
The third, cheaper, was on the sixth floor with no lift.
I gave up before even reaching the top, thinking about my future boxes.
That evening I sent off my file for the studio: ID, pay slips, guarantor.
Three days later the agency rang me to say it had been accepted.
I'm signing the lease on Friday and moving in the following weekend, check-in report in hand.

lessons.title: Colocation
lessons.description: Share a flat without falling out: divide the chores, split the bills and negotiate the house rules.

blocks.heading: Who does what: chores and the rota
blocks.body: Flat-sharing vocabulary revolves around les corvées, the unglamorous jobs nobody wants. The standard solution is un planning, a rota, and the key phrase is à tour de rôle, meaning in turn. Note that French says faire le ménage, faire la vaisselle, faire la lessive and sortir les poubelles — all with faire except the bins.

examples.french: On a affiché un planning des corvées sur le frigo.
examples.english: We've put a chore rota up on the fridge.

examples.french: Chacun fait le ménage à tour de rôle.
examples.english: Each of us does the cleaning in turn.

examples.french: C'est à toi de sortir les poubelles ce soir.
examples.english: It's your turn to take the bins out tonight.

examples.french: Personne ne fait jamais la vaisselle le dimanche.
examples.english: Nobody ever does the washing-up on Sundays.

examples.french: On se partage les parties communes équitablement.
examples.english: We share the communal areas fairly.

examples.french: La salle de bains est un vrai bazar depuis lundi.
examples.english: The bathroom has been a total mess since Monday.

blocks.tip: C'est à toi de + infinitive is the cleanest way to say it's your turn to. C'est ton tour works too, but sounds more like a game.

blocks.heading: Money: splitting the bills
blocks.body: Sharing a flat means constant small transfers. Répartir means to divide up, and the standard formula is on partage en trois or chacun paie sa part. Many flat-shares keep une caisse commune, a kitty, for shared shopping. To ask for your money back, use rembourser: tu me rembourses quand tu peux.

examples.french: On répartit les factures selon la taille des chambres.
examples.english: We divide the bills according to the size of the rooms.

examples.french: Chacun paie sa part du loyer le premier du mois.
examples.english: Each of us pays our share of the rent on the first of the month.

examples.french: J'ai avancé l'argent des courses, tu me rembourseras.
examples.english: I fronted the money for the shopping, you'll pay me back.

examples.french: On met vingt euros chacun dans la caisse commune.
examples.english: We each put twenty euros into the kitty.

examples.french: La facture d'électricité était salée ce trimestre.
examples.english: The electricity bill was steep this quarter.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas équitable si je paie toujours pour tout le monde.
examples.english: It isn't fair if I always pay for everyone.

blocks.tip: Salé literally means salty; applied to a bill or a price it means painfully high. Very common in speech.

blocks.heading: Raising a problem without a row
blocks.body: The French art of raising an issue is to soften the opening and stay factual. Start with je ne veux pas faire d'histoires, mais… or ça m'embête un peu de te dire ça, then describe the behaviour rather than attacking the person. Reprocher quelque chose à quelqu'un is to reproach someone for something — note the à. Finish by proposing a compromis.

examples.french: Je ne veux pas faire d'histoires, mais la cuisine est encore sale.
examples.english: I don't want to make a fuss, but the kitchen is dirty again.

examples.french: Ça m'embête un peu de te le dire, mais tu rentres très tard.
examples.english: It's a bit awkward to tell you, but you come home very late.

examples.french: Je ne te reproche rien, je voudrais juste qu'on en parle.
examples.english: I'm not blaming you for anything, I'd just like us to talk about it.

examples.french: On pourrait trouver un compromis sur le bruit après minuit.
examples.english: We could find a compromise about noise after midnight.

examples.french: Mettons les choses au clair une bonne fois pour toutes.
examples.english: Let's clear things up once and for all.

examples.french: Franchement, je préfère qu'on se dise tout tout de suite.
examples.english: Honestly, I'd rather we told each other everything straight away.

blocks.tip: Faire des histoires means to make a fuss. Saying je ne veux pas faire d'histoires first buys you a lot of goodwill before the complaint.

blocks.heading: The subjunctive after necessity and wanting
blocks.body: House rules are the natural home of the subjunctive. Any expression of necessity, will or emotion followed by que triggers it: il faut que, je voudrais que, j'aimerais que, ça m'énerve que, je ne supporte pas que. Form it from the ils stem of the present: ils rangent gives que je range, ils partent gives que je parte. Learn the four irregulars that matter here by heart: que je sois, que j'aie, que je fasse, que j'aille.

blocks.heading: Negotiating politely with the conditional
blocks.body: To ask a flatmate for something without sounding like a manager, use the conditional. Tu pourrais, ça t'ennuierait de, il vaudrait mieux and on pourrait all soften a demand. Ça t'ennuierait de + infinitive literally means would it bother you to, and it is the most useful phrase in this lesson. Note that on pourrait presents the solution as shared rather than imposed.

For three weeks the atmosphere in the flat had become heavy.

Adrien admitted that he systematically forgot to take the bins out.
As for me, I confessed that I left my things lying around in the communal areas.
We wrote a proper set of house rules, in three points, on a sheet taped to the fridge.
Firstly, a chore rota, everyone in turn, no exceptions.

Thirdly, a kitty of thirty euros per person for cleaning products.
It wasn't perfect, but it was a compromise everyone could keep to.

I wouldn't say we've become friends, but we get on much better than before.

lessons.title: Aménager
lessons.description: Do up your flat, describe repairs and call in a tradesperson — the home of faire + infinitive.

blocks.heading: Doing the place up
blocks.body: Aménager means to fit out or arrange a space, décorer to decorate. The big jobs are called les travaux, always plural, and while they last the flat is un chantier, a building site. French distinguishes doing it yourself (bricoler) from having it done by an artisan. Refaire is the everyday verb for redoing anything: refaire la cuisine, refaire l'électricité.

examples.french: On a aménagé le bureau sous les combles.
examples.english: We fitted out the office in the loft space.

examples.french: Les travaux devraient durer trois semaines.
examples.english: The works should last three weeks.

examples.french: C'est un vrai chantier, on mange par terre.
examples.english: It's a total building site, we're eating on the floor.

examples.french: J'aime bricoler le week-end, ça me détend.
examples.english: I like doing DIY at the weekend, it relaxes me.

examples.french: On va refaire la salle de bains l'an prochain.
examples.english: We're going to redo the bathroom next year.

examples.french: J'ai posé de la moquette dans la chambre.
examples.english: I laid carpet in the bedroom.

blocks.tip: Un chantier used figuratively means a huge unfinished job of any kind: ma thèse, c'est un chantier.

blocks.heading: When something breaks
blocks.body: Two words carry most breakdowns: une panne for anything electrical or mechanical, and une fuite for anything leaking. Something broken is en panne, cassé or hors service (HS in speech). To describe the symptom, use ne… plus: la lumière ne marche plus, l'eau chaude ne coule plus. Then state how long: depuis trois jours.

examples.french: Le chauffe-eau est en panne depuis lundi.
examples.english: The water heater has been broken since Monday.

examples.french: Il y a une fuite sous l'évier de la cuisine.
examples.english: There's a leak under the kitchen sink.

blocks.tip: In a rented flat, small maintenance (l'entretien courant) is the tenant's job, but a broken boiler is the landlord's. Report it by email so you have a written trace.

blocks.heading: Calling in a tradesperson
blocks.body: Before any work, ask for un devis, a written quote, which is normally free and which you must accept in writing. The bill separates les matériaux from la main-d'œuvre, the labour. Standard phrases: pouvez-vous passer cette semaine, vous prenez combien de l'heure, à partir de quand seriez-vous disponible.

examples.english: I'd like to get a plumber to come urgently.

blocks.tip: Un devis signé is legally binding on the price. Never let work start on a verbal estimate — c'est le devis qui fait foi.

blocks.heading: faire + infinitive: having something done
blocks.body: Faire followed directly by an infinitive means to have something done by somebody else — the difference between je repeins la cuisine (I paint it myself) and je fais repeindre la cuisine (I have it painted). Nothing comes between faire and the infinitive: never say je fais la cuisine repeindre. The person doing the job is introduced by par or à: je fais repeindre la cuisine par un peintre.

examples.french: Je fais repeindre le salon la semaine prochaine.
examples.english: I'm having the living room repainted next week.

examples.french: On a fait venir un plombier en urgence.
examples.english: We got a plumber to come urgently.

examples.french: Elle a fait changer la serrure dès son arrivée.
examples.english: She had the lock changed as soon as she arrived.

examples.french: Fais réparer le volet avant l'hiver.
examples.english: Have the shutter repaired before winter.

blocks.tip: In the passé composé, the participle fait never agrees when it is followed by an infinitive: la cuisine que j'ai fait repeindre — no e.

blocks.heading: Related structures: laisser, se faire and faire faire
blocks.body: Laisser + infinitive means to let something happen: j'ai laissé l'artisan entrer. Se faire + infinitive puts you on the receiving end: je me suis fait installer une douche means I had a shower installed for myself. And when the job itself is unnamed, French happily doubles the verb: faire faire des travaux, to have work done. Pronouns go before faire, not before the infinitive: je le fais réparer.

passages.title: Six semaines de chantier
passages.french:
Quand on a récupéré les clés, l'appartement sentait le vieux papier peint et l'humidité.
Mon frère, qui adore bricoler, a promis que tout serait fini en quinze jours.
Ça en a pris six semaines, et je crois qu'il ne me le pardonnera jamais.
On a arraché le papier peint nous-mêmes, poncé les murs et repeint le salon en deux week-ends.
En revanche, on a fait refaire toute l'électricité par un artisan recommandé par la voisine.
Son devis était le plus élevé des trois, mais il était le seul à tout détailler.
J'ai aussi fait changer la serrure, par principe, dès le premier jour.
Le plombier, lui, est passé trois fois avant de trouver d'où venait la fuite.
Pendant tout ce temps, on vivait entre des cartons et une perceuse posée sur la table.
Le soir, on mangeait des pâtes par terre en regardant les murs sécher.
La moquette de la chambre attendra l'an prochain : le budget a fondu plus vite que prévu.
Mais samedi, on pend enfin la crémaillère, avec des chaises empruntées aux voisins.
Et franchement, en refermant la porte le soir, je me dis que ça valait le coup.
passages.english:
When we got the keys, the flat smelled of old wallpaper and damp.
My brother, who loves DIY, promised everything would be finished in a fortnight.
It took six weeks, and I don't think he'll ever forgive me for it.
We stripped the wallpaper ourselves, sanded the walls and repainted the living room over two weekends.
On the other hand, we had all the wiring redone by a tradesman recommended by the neighbour.
His quote was the highest of the three, but he was the only one who itemised everything.
I also had the lock changed, on principle, from day one.
The plumber, for his part, came round three times before finding where the leak was coming from.
All that time, we lived among boxes with a drill sitting on the table.
In the evening we ate pasta on the floor watching the walls dry.
The bedroom carpet will have to wait until next year: the budget melted faster than expected.
But on Saturday we're finally having the housewarming, with chairs borrowed from the neighbours.
And honestly, closing the door in the evening, I tell myself it was worth it.
